Her father would have said the moon was drunk. He had a joke for everything the sea did that it shouldn't. But her father had been gone six years now, and the jokes had gone with him, and the sea kept finding new things to do that it shouldn't.

By nine the water was over the second step of the slipway. By ten the old men who usually sat on the bollards had moved to the café porch and were arguing about whether the almanac had been printed wrong. Mara sold three bags of lugworm to nobody in particular and kept looking at the horizon, where a low grey smudge sat exactly where no island was.

At eleven Tomas came down from the lighthouse on his bicycle, which he never did before noon. He leaned it against her window and didn't come in. He just stood there, looking at the same smudge.

"You see it too," she said through the glass.

"I've been seeing it since four," he said. "That's when the light went out."

Not away. Down, the way a man sits when he's told a thing will take a while. It settled at her heel and stayed, and the lean went out of the dark the way lean goes out of a rope when both ends are made fast. It wasn't pulling now. It was waiting.

"It's sat," Aldo said. "Ines. Is it wet?"

"No." Her voice was thin. "It's not drier either."

"Then it's listening to her."

Mara looked at the card. Light kept. A man walks into a lighthouse. Her father had said the first line to the dark and rowed into it, and the dark had taken the rest on credit. She had told it there'd be an end. Now there had to be one.

She didn't know the end. She knew him. She knew how he stood at the counter with a tub of lugworm and let a customer wait.

"A man walks into a lighthouse," she said.

Nothing moved. Her ankle was warm and nothing else was.

"Keeper says, we're closed. Light's out."

Tomas made a sound that was not a word.

"Man says, I know. I could see that from the water." She stopped. The stop was his; she'd heard him do it a hundred times, the pause that was the joke and not the words. "Keeper says, then what did you come up for."

The dark did not lean. It held the stop with her.

Under Ines's palm the thwart stayed dry. But at the edge of the dry patch, along the line of her smallest finger, the leather darkened a thread's width.
